new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive and not predictable; it may fall on the final syllable (open or closed), an open penult, or an open antepenult, but not on a closed penult or closed antepenult. A stressed open penult is phonetically lengthened. Certain suffixes and enclitics (PV -en, specificity =i, enclitic pronouns, perfective <in>, stative me-) shift stress one syllable rightward.
new_statements.secondary_stress: When an enclitic pronoun attracts primary stress to the new ultima, secondary stress may remain on the original stressed syllable (now antepenult), with lengthening and lowering of /i/ (sec. 3.2.7.3.2, ex. 3.41 [mənlaˌtɪ:=ʔa'mi]).
new_statements.exceptions: Some minimal pairs may be due to borrowing (e.g. /ma'ta/ 'eye' probably Tagalog); closed penults and closed antepenults never bear stress; author suggests NAlta lost inherited PPh contrastive accent and redeveloped it via borrowing, but says more data are needed; stress marking in the glossary is not consistent across all entries.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word (roots and affixed/cliticized phonological words); data from a corpus of recordings, minimal pairs found via ELAN searches; stress shift discussed for derived words and host+enclitic phonological words.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Northern Alta [aqn], glottocode nort2875 (alternative names given: Edimala, Baler Negrito, Ditaylin Alta/Dumagat), as spoken in Diteki, Dicoliat, Dianed and Villa Aurora barangays, Aurora Province, Luzon; no dialect split is made for the stress description. Not to be confused with Southern Alta (Kabuloan, sout2905).

new_statements.relation_note: Same source and same reading as the existing statement ('lexical (unpredictable)'); the catalog record itself has an empty rule, and this read-all pass fills it in and adds detail: the attested stress positions (ultima open/closed, open penult, open antepenult; no closed penult/antepenult), penult lengthening under stress, the affix- and clitic-triggered stress shifts of sec. 3.2.6, and the one explicit secondary-stress observation (p. 71).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive and cannot be predicted from the shape of the word: it may fall on the ultima (open or closed), on an open penult, or on an open antepenult; stressed closed penults and closed antepenults are unattested (Table 2.2). A stressed open penult is lengthened (vowels /i a u/ lengthen, schwa does not). The author suggests (pp. 33-34) that Northern Alta lost the inherited Proto-Philippine contrastive accent and re-acquired contrastive stress through borrowing, but says more data are needed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned once, in liaison: 'the 1pe.ABS Pronoun =ʔami, attracts stress to the ultima but secondary stress remains on the original ultima syllable, which is now antepenult, triggering lengthening and lowering of /i/' - /mәnlati=ʔa'mi/ [mәnla,tɪ:=ʔa'mi] 'we work with rattan' (p. 71, ex. 3.41). Sec. 2.3 (p. 23, PDF 44) notes that secondary stress may be represented in phonetic transcriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts under affixation and cliticisation (sec. 3.2.6, pp. 67-68, Table 3.14): the suffixes -an / -әn and the specificity enclitic =i attract stress to the ultima ('in all cases, stress is attracted to the ultima as a result of the affixation', p. 58); the stative prefix mә- and the perfective infix <in> move stress one syllable to the left (pp. 70-71, exx. 3.38-3.40); enclitic pronouns attract stress to the ultima of the host (p. 71). Some minimal pairs are attributed to borrowing (/ma'ta/ 'eye' probably Tagalog; /'kaja/ possibly Tagalog or Ilokano, fn. 4-5, p. 32). Where a suffix does not shift stress, the newly penultimate stressed vowel is lengthened (sec. 3.2.7.2, p. 69).
new_statements.identity_note: The dissertation documents Northern Alta [aqn] as a single language; no dialect is singled out in the stress sections. The author notes (pp. 33-34) that Northern Alta does not reflect Proto-Philippine penultimate length and may have lost and then re-acquired contrastive accent through borrowing from Tagalog/Ilokano, so several of the cited minimal pairs involve loanwords.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.2 (p.32-34): lexical accent is phonemic (minimal pairs /'mata/ 'ripe' vs /ma'ta/ 'eye' etc.); stress may fall on open or closed ultima, open penult, or open antepenult (never a closed penult/antepenult); stressed open penults are lengthened; NAlta does not reflect PPh accent. Sec. 3.2.6 (p.67-68): certain suffixes/enclitics (-en, =i, pronouns, <in>, me-) shift stress rightward; secondary stress may remain on the original ultima. Sec. 9.1.5.2 (p.351): 'the position of the stress syllable in a word cannot be predicted', so the glossary marks stress with an acute.
